title: UX & Human‐Centred Design Playbook
content: This playbook turns product-design thinking into concrete principles, guidance, cheat sheets, and checklists for agents, engineers and designers who want to build products people trust and enjoy using, or at the very least do not find frustrating. Use it as a working standard for ScribeFloat products and as a reference when building new interfaces.

chapters.title: How to read this playbook
chapters.content:
Read this once to understand the standard we are aiming for across ScribeFloat products.
You do not need to memorise every rule. The aim is to build shared judgement around what good UX looks like in our context: professional, dense, trustworthy, fast, accessible, and clear.
After reading it, use the playbook as a reference when designing, building, or reviewing an interface. If something feels unclear, slow, inconsistent, hard to scan, or awkward to use, check the relevant section and use it to make a better decision.

chapters.title: Know Your User
chapters.content: Understand who is using the product, what they are trying to do, and what helps them do it quickly and without friction. Answer these four questions before building anything:

items.title: Who is this for?
items.content: What do they need to do, and how familiar are they with the workflow?

items.title: What's the task?
items.content: Research? Review? Analysis? Drafting? Workflow management? Content creation? Configuration?

items.title: What density?
items.content: Power-user tools need comfortable density. First-time setup flows can be more spacious.

items.title: What does success look like?
items.content: The user accomplishes their task faster and with more confidence than before.

items.title: Professional and trustworthy:
items.content: a serious tool for serious work.

items.title: Neutral and calm:
items.content: restrained, clear, and dependable, not loud or overdesigned.

items.title: Snappy and frictionless:
items.content: common workflows move immediately, without clunky steps or unnecessary waiting.

items.title: Quietly premium:
items.content: polished and refined, never flashy or consumer-grade.

items.title: Dense but scannable:
items.content: knowledge workers work with a lot of text and data, so the UI should fit a lot in without becoming messy.

items.title: Warm but serious:
items.content: the accent brand colour softens the neutral base without making the product feel like a generic SaaS dashboard.

items.title: Consistent:
items.content: the same things work the same way across the product.

sections.title: What ScribeFloat tools must avoid
table: Consumer-app aesthetics, such as playful illustrations, bubbly shapes, gamification
Undermines trust. knowledge workers need to feel they are using a professional instrument.
Marketing-site patterns, such as hero sections, gradient backgrounds, testimonial cards
These are internal working tools, not products being sold.
Wastes screen real estate that power users need for data. knowledge workers do not want to scroll through cards with 32px padding to find what they are looking for.
The brand fonts are fixed. Decoration competes with content.
Multiple accent colours or rainbow status indicators

Reserve **brand** for the single primary CTA per view. **destructive** is for live recording and danger. **active**, **warning**, **success**, and **focus** each have a defined job — no decorative misuse. Simplicity builds trust.

sections.title: The litmus test
sections.content: At 11pm, would a product designer open this without hesitation, confident it will be fast, clear, and worth using? Does it feel neutral, trustworthy, and snappy, with the important information visible and the workflow frictionless? Does it feel like a tool built for their specific needs rather than a generic SaaS product?

chapters.title: Principles
chapters.content: These are the product principles behind the rest of the playbook. They apply broadly, but ScribeFloat raises the bar on how tightly they need to be applied.

sections.title: 1. Respect the user's time
sections.content: Every extra click, unnecessary animation, and vague label costs someone time. The best interfaces stay out of the way.

sections.title: 2. Reduce cognitive load
sections.content: People have limited working memory. Do not make them hold information between steps, weigh 20 options when 5 will do, or make decisions the system could make for them.

sections.title: 3. Be honest and predictable
sections.content: Interfaces earn trust through consistency. The same action should produce the same result. Buttons should look like buttons. Destructive actions should feel weighty. Feedback should be immediate and truthful. If something is AI-generated, or if a workflow has data-handling limits, say so clearly.

sections.title: 4. Design for the real context
sections.content: Know who your users are, what device they are on, how much time they have, and what they are trying to accomplish. In ScribeFloat's context, this usually means a knowledge workers on a laptop, capturing conversations quickly and reliably so they can focus on the conversation not on notes, recording a transcript, or dictating text or making a decision. Design for that, not for a hypothetical first-time visitor on mobile.

sections.title: 5. Progressive disclosure over upfront complexity
sections.content: Show what is needed at each step. Let complexity reveal itself as the user goes deeper. Break long processes into stages. Use sensible defaults so most users never need to touch advanced settings.

sections.title: 6. Feedback is non-negotiable
sections.content: Every interaction needs visible feedback. Clicked a button? Show it. Submitted a form? Confirm it. Something failed? Explain it where it failed, not in a toast 300px away.

sections.title: 7. Optimise for the common case
sections.content: Optimising for the common case is mostly a hierarchy problem. Lead users clearly through the main workflows, then keep secondary actions, settings, and edge-case options available with less visual weight. Do not make everything compete equally for attention.

sections.title: 8. Use familiar patterns
sections.content: This is where Jakob's Law matters. Do not invent novelty for its own sake. If users already know how to work through something in tools they use every day, like Notion, Slack, and native macOS apps, borrow those patterns where they fit so the product is faster to learn.

sections.title: 9. Show the explanation when it matters
sections.content: In high-stakes workflows, time is too valuable to make the interface cryptic. If someone needs context to use a feature properly, show it in the interface. Do not hide essential explanation in tooltips.

sections.title: 10. Absorb complexity on the engineering side
sections.content:
Every system has complexity. The question is whether the user carries it or the system does. Accept flexible inputs, handle edge cases well, and do the hard work so the interface stays simple.
The next sections turn these principles into interaction, visual, and review guidance.

chapters.title: Interaction & Input
chapters.content: These rules make software easier to learn, safer to use, and faster to trust. In ScribeFloat, the stakes are higher: errors are costly, feedback matters, and the main path should feel immediate.

items.title: Label clicks should focus the input.
items.content: Wrap inputs with `<label>` or use `htmlFor`.

items.title: Wrap inputs in a `<form>`
items.content: so users can submit by pressing Enter. It is still one of the best interaction patterns on the web.

items.title: Use the correct `type` attribute:
items.content: `email`, `password`, `url`, `tel`, etc. This gives users the right mobile keyboard and enables browser autofill.

items.title: Use `inputMode` when `type` alone is not enough.
items.content: A date-of-birth field should use `type="text"` with `inputMode="numeric"` because it gets a numeric keyboard without the spinner arrows that `type="number"` adds.

items.title: Disable `spellcheck` and `autocomplete`
items.content: on inputs where they are unhelpful, such as codes, IDs, and search queries. Leave them on for free-text fields.

items.title: Use semantic validation attributes
items.content: such as `required`, but provide clear inline validation messages where the product needs more control or clearer wording.

items.title: Never block paste
items.content: on inputs or textareas. Users paste passwords, addresses, and codes constantly.

items.title: Position prefix/suffix icons absolutely
items.content: on top of the input with padding, not adjacent to it. Disable `pointer-events` on decorative icons so clicking them focuses the input underneath.

items.title: Let textareas grow with their content.
items.content: Use `field-sizing: content` with `min-height` and `max-height` constraints so textareas expand as the user types and shrink when content is removed. This avoids forcing users to scroll inside a tiny fixed box or manually resize. Pair with `resize-none` since the browser handles sizing.

items.title: Disable buttons after submission
items.content: to prevent duplicate requests. Show a loading spinner if the user is waiting for a network response. In fast professional workflows, users often double-click instinctively, so protect them from it.

items.title: Toggles take effect immediately:
items.content: no confirmation step. If something needs confirmation, it is not a toggle. It is a setting with a save button.

items.title: Display success feedback relative to its trigger.
items.content: A successful copy should show a temporary checkmark on the button, not a toast notification in the corner. A form error should highlight the relevant input, not the entire form.

items.title: Optimistically update low-risk, reversible actions
items.content: and roll back on server error. For destructive, legal, confidential, or high-impact actions, show clear pending, confirmed, and failed states instead of pretending the action has completed.

items.title: Confirm before destroying user effort.
items.content: If the user invested time creating something like a document, an unsaved draft, or a saved search, deleting it should require confirmation. Low-effort changes, like filter selections, do not need confirmation because they are quick to recreate.

items.title: Cancel stale requests when the user moves on.
items.content: If a user starts a new search, navigation, or AI query before the previous one finishes, abort the in-flight request and start the new one immediately. Do not queue them or make the user wait. Use `AbortController` to wire this up, and make sure abort cleanup covers any timers or streaming connections tied to the original request.

items.title: Disable `user-select`
items.content: on button labels and interactive element content. Users clicking a button do not want to accidentally select its text.

items.title: Decorative elements
items.content: (glows, gradients, overlays) should have `pointer-events: none` so they don't intercept clicks.

items.title: Menus should feel immediate on pointer interaction.
items.content: Prefer established accessible menu components, and avoid adding delays that make the UI feel sluggish.

items.title: Focusable elements in sequential lists
items.content: (search results, menu items, file lists) should support keyboard navigation with arrow keys.

sections.title: Filters
sections.content: When multiple filters can be changed in quick succession and each change triggers a network request, the interface needs to balance responsiveness with efficiency.

items.title: Update the filter UI immediately, debounce the network call.
items.content: When a user toggles a checkbox, selects a dropdown option, or changes a date range, reflect the change in the UI instantly so it feels responsive. Batch the actual API call behind a debounce (500–800ms works well) so rapid multi-filter changes produce a single request, not five.

items.title: Bypass debounce for reset actions.
items.content: "Clear all filters" should fire immediately. The user chose a decisive action and should not wait for a timer. Cancel any pending debounced call at the same time.

items.title: Skip redundant requests.
items.content: Before applying debounced filters, compare the new state against the current active state. If nothing actually changed, do not fire the request. This avoids unnecessary round-trips when the user toggles a filter on and back off within the debounce window.

items.title: Only debounce when the cost justifies it.
items.content: If filters do not trigger network requests (e.g. client-side filtering on a small dataset), apply them immediately. The debounce is there to protect against expensive server calls, not to add latency for its own sake.

sections.title: Explanations, AI, and data handling
sections.content: Treat these as one rule: guide the main path inline, explain risky states where they appear, and frame AI output clearly enough that users know what it is and what still needs checking.

items.title: Use hierarchy to guide the user through the main workflow.
items.content: Put the most common path front and centre, then keep less common actions and settings available with less visual weight.

items.title: Show important explanation in the interface.
items.content: If a user needs a piece of information to understand what a feature does, what a result means, or what will happen next, show it inline.

items.title: Use tooltips for extra help, not core meaning.
items.content: Tooltips are appropriate for additional information, repeated object descriptions, or compact UIs where many items need the same kind of explanation.

items.title: Clearly label AI-generated information.
items.content: If a summary, suggestion, classification, or draft is AI-generated, say so directly in the UI.

items.title: Tell users what they still need to verify.
items.content: AI output should help them move faster, but the interface should make it clear when they still need to check for inaccuracies or use their own judgement.

items.title: State the app's data clearance clearly.
items.content: Users should not have to guess whether they can put confidential conversations or meeting recordings into the product.

items.title: Put data-handling guidance near the point of use.
items.content: If an input has restrictions, or if a workflow is approved only for certain classes of data, show that where the user is making the decision.

chapters.title: Typography
chapters.content:
Typography is not decoration. It determines whether information feels legible, structured, and credible before anyone reads a full sentence.
In dense professional tools, typography is the first filter for what matters. Weak hierarchy makes timestamps, speaker labels, audio duration, and file paths disappear into the page.

items.text: Apply `-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased` for crisp rendering on high pixel-density screens.
Apply `text-rendering: optimizeLegibility` for better kerning and ligatures.
Subset fonts based on the content, relevant alphabet, or languages used. Do not ship 200KB of glyphs you will never render.

items.title: Never use font weights below 400.
items.content: Light weights from 100 to 300 are unreadable on most screens.

items.title: Medium headings look best at 500-600 weight.
items.content: Reserve 700, bold, for emphasis or primary headings.

items.title: Font weight must not change on hover or selection.
items.content: Changing weight causes layout shift because the text physically moves. Use `color`, `background`, or `text-decoration` instead.

sections.title: Hierarchy
sections.content:
ScribeFloat uses five named scale steps. Use the semantic class (or `.sf-*` helper) — never compose the parts individually.

Hierarchy comes from size, case, and opacity only. No bold (`font-weight` 600+). No custom tracking outside the three defined values (`tracking-normal`, `tracking-tight`, `tracking-stamped`).
table: Large numeric readout. One per screen.
Modal titles, screen headers — one per view
Form field labels, button text, accordion titles
Section dividers, status chips, file sizes, hotkey chips

items.text: Use `text-balance` on headings to prevent awkward line breaks.
Use `text-pretty` on body paragraphs for better widows/orphans handling.
Use `tabular-nums` for any numerical data so digits align in columns.
Use `truncate` or `line-clamp` in dense layouts to prevent text overflow.
Format long numbers and IDs in readable chunks: `4242 4242 4242 4242`, not `4242424242424242`.

chapters.title: Motion & Animation
chapters.content: Good motion explains change. It should show state, direction, and feedback without slowing people down.

sections.title: Timing
sections.content: Interactions should feel immediate. Anything over 150ms for direct manipulation, like hover or press, will feel sluggish.
table: Almost never. If it's this slow, question whether you need the animation at all.

sections.title: Scale & proportion
sections.content:
Animation values should be proportional to the element's size:
Small elements need small motion. Large elements can tolerate slightly more, but still less than you think.

items.title: Don't
items.content: scale a dialog from `0 → 1`. Fade opacity and scale from `~0.95`.

items.title: Don't
items.content: scale a button press from `1 → 0.8`. Use `~0.96` or `~0.98`.

items.title: Don't
items.content: slide a tooltip in from 50px away. Use `4-8px`.

sections.title: When to skip animation
sections.content:
Some interactions are better with no motion at all. Frequent, low-novelty actions should be instant:
The native macOS context menu only animates _out_, not _in_, because it gets used so often. The same logic applies here. Animation should serve the user, not entertain the developer.

items.text: Opening a context menu or right-click menu
Adding or removing items from a list
Hovering trivial or utility buttons
Switching tabs in a familiar interface

sections.title: Purpose
sections.content: If an animation does not serve one of these, remove it.
table: Drawer sliding in from the edge, dropdown expanding
Error state drawing attention, new item highlighting
Tab content crossfading, accordion expanding in place

sections.title: Reduced motion

chapters.title: Responsive
chapters.content: Responsive design is not just shrinking layouts. It is preserving clarity, control, and task flow as space changes.

sections.title: Responsive design
sections.content: In ScribeFloat, most tools are laptop-first. Do not design around mobile as the main case, but make sure layouts still work at narrower widths, in split-screen, and in resized laptop windows:

chapters.title: Accessibility
chapters.content: Accessibility is product quality, not a compliance pass. If an interface is harder to perceive, navigate, or understand, it is worse software.

items.text: Use visible focus indicators on all interactive elements. The app uses a global `2px` **focus**-token ring with offset (`ring-focus ring-offset-canvas` in `src/app.css` `@layer base`).
Focusable elements in menus, option lists, and similar sequential collections should support arrow-key navigation.

Do not rebuild keyboard or focus behaviour from scratch. Use native HTML elements and established component libraries that already handle this well. In MUI, prefer components like `MenuList`, `MenuItem`, `Autocomplete`, and `Select` when they fit the pattern.
Icon-only buttons **must** have an explicit `aria-label`.
Decorative elements should use `aria-hidden="true"`. Meaningful complex visuals should have an accessible name, summary, or supporting text.
Images should use `` tags with `alt` text because this enables screen readers and right-click copy.

sections.title: Tooltips
sections.content: Same rule as Interaction & Input: essential explanation belongs in the interface, not behind hover.

items.text: Tooltips triggered by hover **must not contain interactive content** (links, buttons). Users cannot reach them before they disappear.

Disabled buttons **should not have tooltips**. Disabled elements are removed from the tab order, so keyboard users will never trigger the tooltip or know why the button is disabled. Show an inline message instead.
Do not put essential explanation in a tooltip. If users need the information to understand the screen or use the feature correctly, show it inline.
Tooltips work best for extra detail, repeated descriptions, or dense interfaces where many similar objects need short labels or definitions.
Do not rely on colour alone to convey meaning. Pair colour with icons, text, or patterns.
Ensure a minimum contrast ratio of **4.5:1** for body text and **3:1** for large text, WCAG AA.
Test your interface in both light and dark mode.
Use a `<svg>` favicon with a `<style>` tag that adapts to system theme via `prefers-color-scheme`.
Style the text selection state with `::selection`.

chapters.title: Performance & Optimisation
chapters.content: Performance shapes trust as much as visuals do. If an interface looks polished but feels slow or unstable, it is still poorly designed.

items.text: Large `blur()` values on `filter` or `backdrop-filter` are expensive. Use them sparingly.
Scaling and blurring filled rectangles causes banding, so use radial gradients instead.
Animate only `transform` and `opacity` for 60fps compositing. Animating `width`, `height`, `top`, `left`, `margin`, or `padding` triggers layout reflow.
Never interleave DOM reads and writes in the same frame. Batch all reads first, then writes.
Use `transform: translateZ(0)` sparingly if you need to promote elements to their own compositor layer for smoother animation.
Use `will-change` only during active animations. Add it on hover/focus, remove it when done. Pre-emptively adding it everywhere can _hurt_ performance.
Pause off-screen animations with `IntersectionObserver`.

items.title: Reserve space for scrollbars
items.content: with `scrollbar-gutter: stable` on any container that may or may not scroll depending on content length. Without it, the layout shifts horizontally when a scrollbar appears or disappears, which is especially jarring in side-by-side panels, sidebars, and main content areas. Apply it on scrollable containers rather than globally.

items.text: For real-time values that update on every frame (scroll position, waveform data, animation), use a plain variable instead of a `$state` rune to avoid triggering Svelte's reactive graph on every animation frame. Commit to the DOM directly via the canvas API or direct element mutations.
Use `$derived` for computed values that depend on reactive state. Avoid recalculating inside `$effect` when `$derived` would do.
For CPU-bound work (audio processing, large transcripts), use `requestAnimationFrame` or Tauri backend commands to keep the main thread free.
Use structural skeleton screens that match the layout they will replace, not generic spinners.
Optimistically update the UI on user actions and roll back on error.
Productivity improves when response time stays under 400ms. Provide instant visual feedback for every interaction.

chapters.title: Visual Design & Layout
chapters.content: Visual design is how hierarchy becomes obvious at a glance. ScribeFloat needs a restrained, information-rich version of it.

sections.title: Surfaces & depth
sections.content:
**Dark mode:** lighter surface = higher elevation. Surface colour stepping alone communicates depth — no shadows on inner elements.
**Light mode:** darker surface = higher elevation. Same token names; CSS vars swap automatically via the `data-theme` attribute on the root.

Elevation is never communicated by shadow weight or border thickness. Only the top-level floating panel (PanelShell) uses a drop shadow.
table: Page / window background only. Never a container.
Cards, note items, waveform bg, dividers.

items.text: Keep the surface treatment consistent: same border radius, same padding, same edge definition.
Internal structure varies by content type:

items.title: Data cards:
items.content: Dense, tabular, small text, minimal padding. _Example: matter list items, document metadata._

items.title: Summary cards:
items.content: Clear headline number, supporting context below. _Example: deal value, document count, deadline countdown._

items.title: Action cards:
items.content: Clear CTA, brief description, minimal distraction. _Example: "Start new research" prompt in an empty state._

items.text: Do not over-card. If everything is in a card, nothing has hierarchy. Use cards for distinct, self-contained units of information.

sections.title: Spacing
sections.content: Use a consistent spacing scale based on a 4px grid:

items.text: Use **semantic colour tokens**, not raw hex or OKLCH literals. Every token is defined in `src/app.css` (`--sf-*` / `@theme inline`) and switches automatically between dark and light mode.

**Brand** (`bg-brand` / `text-on-brand`) for the single primary action button per screen. **Destructive** for recording status dot and danger actions. **Active** for selection and on-states (e.g. tabs, toggle on). **Focus** for keyboard focus rings only. **Warning** and **success** for caution and done — not interchangeable.

Build in grey surfaces first; add state colour only when it carries meaning. Do not use **brand** for waveform bars or decorative accents; do not use **active** as the keyboard focus substitute for **focus**.
Semantic colours must stay semantically correct. Do not use **brand** as a decorative accent, or **success** for waveform bars. Pair colour with text or icon so meaning is never colour-only.

sections.title: Border radius
sections.content: ScribeFloat uses three fixed radius values. Do not introduce others — this is an instrument, not a consumer app.
table: Chips, small tags, status dot containers, inner card elements
Buttons, inputs, cards, panels, modals — everything else
Toggle knob and recording status dot only. Nothing else.

sections.title: Scroll overflow cues
sections.content: In dense layouts, users need to know when content extends beyond the visible area. A gradient fade at the top or bottom edge of a scrollable container signals "there is more" without taking up space or adding a permanent scrollbar.

items.text: Fade masks should be `pointer-events: none` so they never block interaction with the content underneath.
Show or hide each mask based on scroll position: top mask appears when scrolled down, bottom mask appears when there is more content below.
Match the gradient colour to the container's background using the same surface token, so the fade blends naturally in both light and dark mode.
Use a `ResizeObserver` alongside scroll events to recalculate when the container or its content changes size.
Marketing-site styling in working tools: oversized hero treatments, decorative gradients, testimonial-style cards, or large areas of empty space that steal room from useful content.
Visual novelty that competes with the task: multiple accent colours, decorative iconography, playful shapes, or rainbow status systems.
Card overload: if every object gets the same container, padding, and weight, nothing feels important.

chapters.title: Data Presentation
chapters.content:
Data presentation is not about putting numbers on a screen. It is about making meaning, relevance, and next steps obvious.
A number alone is not enough. The question is what it means and what the user should do next. "42 of 156 documents reviewed, 27%" is more useful than "42 documents".

items.text: Use `tabular-nums` so digits align in columns. This is critical for financial data, dates, and document counts.
Format long IDs and numbers in readable chunks (matter IDs, reference numbers, monetary amounts).
Show relative context, such as percentages, trends, and comparisons, not just raw values. "$2.3B, up 12% from Q3" beats "$2,300,000,000".
Use `truncate` or `line-clamp` for long text in dense layouts because document titles and party names can be extremely long.
If something is AI-generated, label it clearly. Do not make users infer that a summary, draft, answer, score, or recommendation came from AI.
Show what the AI result is based on where possible, such as source documents, cited inputs, timestamps, or confidence signals.
Make it clear when the user still needs to verify the result for accuracy.
Do not present AI output with the same visual certainty as confirmed facts, system records, or human-reviewed content unless it has actually been checked.
State clearly what kinds of information the app is approved to handle.
If users are allowed to enter confidential or private information, say that clearly. If they are not, say that just as clearly.
Put data clearance guidance near inputs, uploads, and workflows where the decision matters.

sections.title: Empty, loading, and error states
sections.content: Every data-driven view needs loading, empty, and error states. knowledge workers will hit all three often:
table: Structural skeletons matching the layout they'll replace
Document list skeleton with rows, not a spinner
Clear message and one obvious next action
"No results for this matter. Try broadening your search or check the matter ID."
Explain what happened, show it at the point of failure, offer retry
"Failed to load document. Retry" inline, not a page-level error

items.title: Success:
items.content: show relative to the trigger (checkmark on button, not a distant toast).

items.title: Errors:
items.content: highlight the specific input that failed, not the whole form.

items.title: Progress:
items.content: show progress bars, step indicators, or completion percentages for multi-step processes. Motivation increases as users get closer to their goal (Goal-Gradient Effect.

chapters.title: UX Laws Cheat Sheet
chapters.content: You do not need to memorise these. Use them when something feels harder to use than it should and you need to work out why.

sections.title: Interaction & Input
table: Time to reach a target depends on distance and size
Make primary actions large and position them where users already are
Decision time increases with the number of choices
Reduce options, use defaults, break complex tasks into steps
People get more done when the system responds in under 400ms
Provide instant feedback: skeletons, optimistic UI, spinners
Be liberal in what you accept, conservative in what you send
Accept varied input formats, output clean consistent results

sections.title: Perception & Grouping
table: Nearby elements are perceived as related
Group related controls with whitespace between unrelated groups
Similar-looking elements feel like they belong together
Use cards, borders, backgrounds to visually group content
If a design needs explanation, simplify it

sections.title: Memory & Cognition
table: Chunk long lists, limit tabs, break up large forms
Reduce decisions, use familiar patterns, carry data forward
Users expect your site to work like tools they already know
Reuse familiar patterns from tools like Notion, Slack, and native macOS apps where they fit
Users bring expectations from other tools
Match existing patterns before inventing new ones

sections.title: Attention & Recall
table: Use visual emphasis sparingly. If everything stands out, nothing does
First and last items are best remembered
Put important actions at the start and end of lists and toolbars
Use progress indicators and checklists to drive completion

sections.title: Decision Making
table: Too many options slow people down
Limit visible options, use smart defaults, offer curation
The simplest solution is usually the best
Between two designs, choose fewer elements, fewer steps
Most users will not read instructions
Make interfaces self-explanatory with inline hints and progressive disclosure

sections.title: Experience & Motivation
table: Better-looking interfaces often feel easier to use
Visual polish builds trust and forgiveness for minor issues
Experiences are judged by peak moments and the ending
Polish key moments: first use, task completion, error recovery
Show progress bars and step indicators in multi-step flows
People work best when they are not being interrupted

sections.title: Complexity & Effort
table: Complexity cannot be removed, only shifted
Absorb complexity on the engineering side
80% of usage comes from 20% of features
Tasks expand to fill available time
Set expectations with deadlines, limits, and progress indicators

chapters.title: Do's & Don'ts
chapters.content: If you are moving quickly, this is the short version. Use it while building or reviewing a screen. It speeds up common decisions; it does not replace the reasoning above.

sections.title: Interaction
table: Submit forms on Enter via `<form>` wrapping
Require users to find and click a submit button
Disable buttons after submission and show loading
Show success feedback at the trigger location
Show a generic toast notification for everything
Add avoidable delay to frequent menu interactions
Force users to Tab through every item
Wait for the server round-trip to show every low-risk change
Present AI output as if it were confirmed fact
State what data the app can handle
Make users guess what they are allowed to enter
Cancel stale requests when the user starts a new one
Queue requests or make users wait for the previous to finish
Let textareas grow with content using `field-sizing: content`
Force users into a fixed-height textarea with a scrollbar

sections.title: Typography
table: Change font weight on hover, which causes layout shift
Ship unsubsetted fonts with unused glyphs

sections.title: Motion
table: Animate everything because it looks nice
Scale proportionally to element size, such as 0.96, not 0.5
Scale dialogs from 0 or buttons to 0.8
Skip animation on frequent, low-novelty actions
Add entrance animation to context menus

sections.title: Accessibility
table: Rely on surrounding context for meaning
Use CSS background images for content
Show inline text explaining why a button is disabled
Pair colour with icons or text for meaning

sections.title: Layout & Visual
table: Use a consistent spacing scale, based on a 4px grid
Use **brand** for the single primary CTA; use **focus**, **active**, **warning**, **success**, and **destructive** only for their semantic jobs
Introduce extra brand hues or rainbow decorative accents
Handle loading, empty, and error states
Test in both light and dark mode
Use scroll fade masks on clipped containers
Leave users guessing whether content continues

sections.title: Performance
table: Batch DOM reads before DOM writes
Interleave reads and writes in the same frame
Let scrollbar appearance shift the layout

chapters.title: Self-Check Checklists
chapters.content: These checklists are a final review pass. Use them to catch weak hierarchy, unclear feedback, accessibility gaps, and trust issues before someone else does.

sections.title: Before shipping any interface
sections.content:
Run through these checks before handoff, merge, or review. They are there to catch obvious misses early.
#### Hierarchy & structure
#### States & feedback
#### Accessibility
#### Responsive
#### Dark mode
#### Performance
#### Typography
#### Design consistency
#### AI & data handling

items.text: At 11pm, would a product designer open this without hesitation, expecting it to be fast, clear, and worth using?
Does it feel neutral, trustworthy, and specific to knowledge workers work rather than like a generic SaaS product?
Blur your eyes. Can you still tell what's most important?
Are sections visually separated with consistent spacing?
Does the text hierarchy use distinct levels (title → body → subtitle → muted)?
Are related elements grouped? Are unrelated elements separated?
Is the most important action the most prominent element?
Is the important information visible without forcing users to hunt through drawers, tabs, tooltips, or extra clicks?
Does the visual hierarchy lead users through the main workflow first, while keeping secondary actions and settings available but quieter?
Are familiar patterns used where they help users learn the product faster?
Does every interactive element have hover, focus, active, and disabled states?
Does every data view handle loading, empty, and error?
Do buttons show loading state during async operations?
Is success/error feedback shown at the point of action?
Are form errors highlighted on the specific failing input?
Can a tired user move through the common workflow without friction, confusion, or unnecessary pauses?
Is important explanation shown inline when users need it, rather than hidden in tooltips?
Can the entire interface be used with keyboard only?
Do all icon-only buttons have `aria-label`?
Is colour contrast at least 4.5:1 for body text and at least 3:1 for large text?
Does the interface not rely on colour alone for meaning?
Are focus indicators visible and clear?
Is `prefers-reduced-motion` respected?
Are tooltips only being used for additional information, not essential explanation?
[ ]  Does the layout stay usable at narrower widths, in split-screen, and in resized laptop windows?
Do surfaces still layer correctly, with elevation increasing?
Are borders and dividers visible?
Are overlays, such as modals, drawers, and menus, distinguishable from their backdrop?
Is text readable at all hierarchy levels?
Are semantic colours (error, warning, etc.) legible?
Is the initial load fast? Are heavy resources lazy-loaded?
Are animations using `transform`/`opacity` only?
Are off-screen animations paused?
Does the UI feel responsive, with feedback on actions in under 400ms?
Does the main workflow feel snappy rather than slow, clunky, or overbuilt?
Are loading states structural skeletons, not generic spinners?
Are only weights 400+ used?
Is `antialiased` rendering enabled?
Are numbers in `tabular-nums` where they appear in columns?
Is long text handled with `truncate` or `line-clamp`?
Are fonts subsetted for the relevant character set?
Is decorative colour use restrained? One **brand** CTA per view; **focus**, **active**, **warning**, **success**, and **destructive** only where semantically correct?
Are all colours from semantic tokens, not raw values?
Is border radius consistent across same-level elements?
Does the spacing follow a 4px grid?
Are the same patterns used for the same purposes throughout?
Does the interface still feel like a ScribeFloat tool rather than a generic SaaS dashboard?
Is AI-generated content clearly labelled wherever it appears?
Is it clear what the user still needs to verify for accuracy?
Is the app's data clearance clearly stated?
Are data-handling restrictions shown near the point where users enter, upload, or generate sensitive information?

chapters.title: Appendix: ScribeFloat Design DNA
chapters.content: _This playbook is maintained by UX Engineering and Design at ScribeFloat. It is a working standard, not a fixed rulebook. If a rule does not fit the user, workflow, or technical context, raise it, discuss it, and improve the playbook._
table: Use whitespace _intentionally_. Our users work with dense data, so wasted space means wasted productivity.
Simple does not mean sparse. A well-organised dense interface is easier to use than a sparse one that forces extra paging.
Respect the user. Delight in ScribeFloat means speed, accuracy, and reliability, not confetti animations.

Laptop-first. Our primary users are on laptops or large monitors. We do not design around mobile as the main case, but the UI should still hold up at narrower widths, in split-screen, and in resized laptop windows.
Information-rich aesthetic. Every pixel should earn its place by conveying useful information.
